summary: The video side is a scan-time design that does not follow MAME. FG and BG each have a per-pixel pipeline whose VRAM and char-ROM fetch phases are keyed to H-counter bits. Sprites are drawn into a per-line buffer, and the UPL 'orthogonal palette' is a small mux on pen 1 instead of MAME's expanded 0x200+ palette. Nothing is schematic-level, though: no chip-per-module split, no counter or PAL equations, no board net names. A few things follow MAME exactly, such as the guessed 240 Hz sub-CPU IRQ, the per-game decode/HWTYPE variants taken from the driver's address maps and tile callbacks, and a priority mux that reproduces screen_update_ninjakun's layer order. The overall picture is a hand-designed generic core, leaning slightly toward hardware.

findings.signal: scan-time tile pipeline keyed to H counter
findings.note: Each layer runs an 8-phase case on POSH[2:0]: VRAM address at phase 1, char-ROM address at 4, data latch at 7, and one pixel per VCLK. That is a raster-driven fetch pipeline, not MAME's tilemap/tile_info callback abstraction.

findings.signal: orthogonal palette as a pen-1 mux
findings.note: When the sprite pixel is 1, a 4-bit mux outputs the color number instead (POUT[3:0]==1 ? POUT[7:4] : POUT[3:0]). MAME emulates this by expanding and copying palette entries in paletteram_w; the core uses the cheap logic a board would have.

findings.signal: sprite engine: Y-first hit test, then 2x32-bit ROM fetch into a line buffer
findings.note: Each line, the engine reads byte 2 (Y) first, tests the hit with an 8-bit subtract (HV[7:4]==4'b1111), and only then fetches attr, tile and X and two ROM words, drawing 16 pixels into a buffer. MAME's per-frame loop reads attr first and blits whole 16x16 sprites.

findings.signal: sub-CPU IRQ rate copied from MAME's guess
findings.note: CPU1 gets a free-running 240 Hz IRQ, exactly MAME's periodic_int value, instead of a source derived from raster counter bits (the MAME driver itself lists this IRQ source as unknown).

findings.signal: priority mux reproduces MAME's draw order
findings.note: The order is BG-forced, FG cat0, sprites, FG cat1, then BG. That is MAME's layer order (bg, fg cat1, sprites, fg cat0, plus the pkunwar bg category pass) written as a priority mux, not a PROM or board priority circuit.

findings.signal: multi-game HWTYPE variants mirror MAME driver variants
findings.note: The tile-code bit packing for each game matches MAME's per-game tile_info expressions one for one (e.g. code+((attr&0xc0)<<2) becomes {BGVDT[15:14],BGVDT[7:0]}), and the decoders are per-game equality compares against MAME's map ranges. The core is organized around the driver's set of games, not one board's decode logic.
Scroll>>3 is added to the CPU's VRAM address, as in MAME's handlers. Any correct implementation has to share this behavior, so it does not count either way.

findings.signal: A002 sync flags as set/reset latch bits
findings.note: Data bits 7 and 6 act as individual set/clear strobes. MAME instead compares the whole byte (data==0x80, data==0x40). Same function, slightly more latch-like here; weak evidence.

findings.signal: time-multiplexed shared bus and FPGA clocking
findings.note: Both Z80s share one I/O/video bus in alternating 24 MHz phases, and all clocks come from a 48 MHz divider. This is FPGA resource engineering.

findings.signal: generic names, neither board nor MAME
findings.note: Signals are named CS_FGV, FGOPQ, SPRNO, WPAD and so on. These are neither schematic net/chip names nor MAME function names, and there are no modules per board chip or PAL.
